story: Jomfruland is the crest of the Ra, the great end moraine that the retreating ice sheet piled up along the coast of southern Scandinavia at the end of the last ice age. Here the ridge breaks the surface as a low island about seven and a half kilometres long and a kilometre wide; elsewhere it runs on under the sea, east towards Mølen and west to Tromøy, where it comes ashore again. On the seaward side, waves have washed away the fine material and left a beach of rounded stones almost seven kilometres long. The island's Old Norse name, Aur, meant gravel.

Nearly all of the park is water, and much of it is shallow and sunlit. The sea floor carries kelp forest, eelgrass meadows, soft mud and shell sand, nurseries for fish and shellfish that the park calls a blue rainforest. Harbour seals haul out on the skerries. Fifteen islets and stretches of shore, among them the south of Stråholmen, are set aside for nesting seabirds and closed to visitors through the breeding season.

On land, Jomfruland is a farmed landscape of hay meadows, grazed pasture, stone walls and broadleaved woods, where wood anemones flower so thickly in early May that the island served as a location for Liv Ullmann's 1995 film of Kristin Lavransdatter. The island lies on a migration route along the coast, and more than 300 bird species have been seen here; thrush nightingale, common rosefinch and red-backed shrike all breed. A bird station, founded in 1969, works from Øitangen at the northern tip.

About 75 people live on Jomfruland year-round, among many holiday homes. Two white lighthouses stand together in the middle of the island: a brick tower first lit in 1839 and the taller cast-iron tower that replaced it a century later. Protection came piece by piece, with a landscape protection area in 1978, ten small nature reserves on islets and skerries in 1980 and a nature reserve and landscape protection area on Stråholmen in 1990. In December 2016 they were joined with the surrounding sea to form the national park.
howItWorks: Norway's right to roam, allemannsretten, applies on the uncultivated land here: you may walk, swim and pitch a tent without asking, provided you camp at least 150 metres from the nearest house or cabin and leave no trace. From 15 April to 15 September it is illegal across Norway to light a fire in or near woodland, and this park is stricter still: no fire or grill may be lit directly on the ground at any time of year, so use the fire pans provided and bring your own wood. Norway's national lead period for dogs runs from 1 April to 20 August, but here dogs must be kept on a lead all year.

The park's own regulation adds more. Motor traffic on land and ice is banned, as is flying lower than 300 metres; motor-driven model aircraft, which includes drones, may not be used. Boats, including motorboats, may use the park, but from 15 April to 15 July no one may go ashore in the seabird zones or come within 50 metres of their shores by boat, kayak, board or while diving. Tents are not allowed in the seabird zones, on Stråholmen, at Sandbakken or on the farmland at Øitangen. Cycling is allowed only on roads and paths, and electric bicycles and scooters only on the main road to Øitangen. Pebbles may not be taken home, and cairns may not be built on the beach.

Jomfruland is lived in and farmed. Only part of the island lies inside the park; cattle graze it from May to October, a grazing group keeps old-breed sheep on Stråholmen all year, and hay meadows are still cut. Fishing in the sea is allowed all year, and boat sewage may not be emptied into the sea. The park is run by the Jomfruland national park board, and organised activity that could harm the environment, including events for larger groups, needs its permission.

sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-jomfruland: The island itself: a moraine ridge with a pebble beach almost seven kilometres long on the Skagerrak side and sandy coves, meadows and woods on the landward side.
sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-jomfruland-fyr: Two white lighthouses side by side mid-island, a brick tower first lit in 1839 and its cast-iron successor. The old tower can be climbed in summer.
sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-tarntjernet: The island's largest pond, just by the lighthouses. Theodor Kittelsen took inspiration here for his painting «Nøkken», the water spirit of Norwegian folklore.
sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-oitangen: The northern tip of Jomfruland, where the coastal migration of birds passes in spring and autumn and the Jomfruland bird station rings and counts them.
sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-straholmen: A small moraine island two kilometres north of Jomfruland, with no ferry, sheep grazing all year and a seabird reserve in the south, closed 15 April to 15 July.
sightNotes.poi-no-jomfruland-stangnes: The park's one corner on the mainland, at its south-western end and reached by road: smooth ice-scoured rock, shallow sand and kelp just offshore.

entrances: Tårnbrygga on Jomfruland, a ferry quay a short walk from the lighthouses and the visitor centre; not served in strong wind
Aasvik on Jomfruland, the island's other ferry quay
Stangnes, at the south-western end of the park, the only part reached by road
Stråholmen, by taxi boat, kayak or your own boat only
planYourVisit.reservations: There is no entry reservation or permit. Ferries from Kragerø run to a timetable through the year, and Stråholmen is reached by taxi boat, which you book yourself.
permits: Organised activity that could harm the natural environment, including events for larger groups, needs permission from the national park board
Fishing in the sea is allowed all year under the general rules
camping: Wild camping under the right to roam, at least 150 metres from houses and cabins
No tents in the seabird zones, on Stråholmen, at Sandbakken or on the farmland at Øitangen
No fires or grills directly on the ground at any time; use the fire pans provided and bring your own wood

Hotels and guesthouses in Kragerø, on the mainland
seasonalClosures: The seabird zones are closed to landing, and to boats within 50 metres of their shores, from 15 April to 15 July — the zones are signposted; check the park map before you go
The visitor centre on Jomfruland is open daily only in high summer and at weekends in spring — check opening times with the centre before you go

chronology.year: End of the last ice age
chronology.text: The retreating ice sheet lays down the Ra moraine; its crest becomes Jomfruland and Stråholmen.
The island once called Aur, from the Old Norse for gravel, becomes known as Jomfruland.
The brick lighthouse in the middle of the island is first lit.
Theodor Kittelsen draws the island for his Jomfruland series, now in Norway's National Museum.
The Jomfruland bird station is founded; since 1980 it has worked from Øitangen.
Jomfruland is protected as a landscape protection area.
Ten islets and skerries around the island become nature reserves; today they are among the park's seabird zones.
Stråholmen gets a nature reserve and a landscape protection area.
Jomfruland National Park is established on 16 December, covering about 117 square kilometres, 114 of them sea; the rules of seventeen older reserves and protected areas are repealed.

safety: Wear a life jacket in small boats and kayaks. The outer side faces the open Skagerrak, and wind and swell can rise quickly.
Keep well clear of the signposted seabird zones from 15 April to 15 July; disturbed birds leave eggs and chicks exposed to gulls and cold.
The rounded stones of the pebble beach roll underfoot and are slippery when wet. Wear proper shoes.
Cattle graze Jomfruland from May to October. Keep dogs on the lead and close gates behind you.
regulations: No landing in the seabird zones, and no boats within 50 metres of their shores, from 15 April to 15 July.
Dogs on a lead all year.
No fires or grills directly on the ground at any time of year; use the fire pans provided.
No motor traffic on land, no drones or other motor-driven model aircraft, and electric bicycles only on the main road to Øitangen.
Leave the pebbles where they lie: taking stones and building cairns on the beach are not allowed.

weather: This is the Skagerrak coast, and the sea sets the pattern. Spring comes in May, when the wood anemones flower and the spring migration fills the island with birds. Summer is the busy season, with boats in every bay and bathers on the sandy inner shores. Autumn brings the second migration and the first gales; the bird station is staffed from March to November. Winter is quiet, often grey and windy, with few visitors. Wind and swell on the outer side can turn a calm paddle rough within an hour, so watch the forecast in any season.
directions: Jomfruland lies off Kragerø, three to four hours' drive from Oslo or Kristiansand. Kragerø has no railway of its own: the nearest station is Neslandsvatn on the Sørlandet Line between Oslo and Kristiansand, about 27 kilometres away, with buses to Kragerø connecting with some trains. From Kragerø, ferries run year-round to Jomfruland's two quays, Aasvik and Tårnbrygga; there is no public parking on the island, so leave the car on the mainland and walk or cycle. Stråholmen has no ferry, so take a taxi boat from Kragerø, Valle in Bamble or Langesund. Ferry and bus times change with the season, so check Farte or Entur before you travel.
